data.content_ref: inline:The target selects sky view factor (SVF) as the single dominant cross-city modulator of the nighttime UHI gap, but this fails the problem's requirement because the question asks why some cities have a LARGER gap than others 'on a clear, calm night'. The target itself states that low SVF 'slows the nocturnal cooling rate, so the stored thermal mass effect persists longer'. This makes thermal mass/storage the fundamental cause of the temperature gap, and SVF merely a secondary modifier of the cooling rate. If a city has very high thermal mass and anthropogenic heat but open geometry (high SVF), it will still have a large UHI, whereas a low-mass city with low SVF will have a small UHI. Furthermore, on a clear, calm night, wind speeds are negligible, yet wind speed is widely identified as a primary controller of urban-rural temperature differences. By excluding wind speed and thermal mass as the primary modulators, the target presents SVF as the 'single best' explanation, which is mechanistically subordinate to the actual heat storage capacity that dictates the total energy available for nighttime release.
